summary:
Legal gender recognition in Switzerland runs on self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality may change their sex marker, their first name, or both by personal declaration before a civil registrar. No surgery, medical diagnosis or court proceeding is required. About 350 people had used the route in its first months, according to SWI swissinfo reporting of 7 August 2022.

Civil marriage has been open to same-sex couples since 1 July 2022 under the Marriage for All reform, which also opened adoption and IVF and passed a referendum with 64.1% approval. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status can marry in Switzerland and have that marriage recognised on the same terms as any other couple.

Federal criminal law has punished public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds under Article 261bis of the Criminal Code since 1 July 2020. UNHCR's Switzerland guidance records that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited; the criminal provision itself is framed on sexual-orientation grounds.

Reported anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crime is rising. SWI swissinfo, citing LGBTIQ Helpline monitoring, gives roughly six reported hate crimes per week and 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020. These are raw counts of LGBTIQ+ reports generally rather than trans-specific figures, and the sources supply no population denominator. The OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report records that Swiss criminal law contains no general hate-crime provision, that such acts are addressed under the anti-discrimination provision, that recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes, and that police do not record bias motivation.

The Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons 2026-2030 on 28 January 2026. Its three pillars are support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence, with implementation coordinated by the Federal Office for Gender Equality. SWI swissinfo covered the plan's publication in 2026.

Placement of trans detainees is governed cantonally. This record documents no federal provision, no Federal Supreme Court case law and no special trans units. The canton of Basel-Stadt inserted an explicit gender-identity clause into its detention law (JVG) adopted by the Grand Council on 13 November 2019: section 2 requires separation of female and male detainees and states that the detained person's gender identity is respected as far as possible, and the prison directorate may deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority.

Conversion therapy remains unregulated at federal level. The National Council adopted a national ban on 12 December 2022 by 143 votes to 37 with 11 abstentions, and the bill is still pending in the Council of States. Cantonal bans are in force in Neuchâtel (2023), Valais and Vaud (2024). The Federal Council states that such therapies are ineffective and cause significant suffering to young people subjected to them and would breach professional duties, and a 2026 report confirms it condemns the practice while leaving further federal regulation open.

Support services documented in this record include a helpline launched by Swiss LGBT groups in November 2016, Dialogai (founded 1982) offering helplines and advice, and Transgender Network Switzerland, which advises on legal sex and name changes, the armed forces and asylum.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map country page for Switzerland reports an overall index score and per-category compliance ratings assessed after the 2021 self-determination and discrimination votes; the score and ratings themselves are not carried in this inventory.

Blood donation rules moved on 1 November 2023 to a four-month deferral after last new sexual contact for gay men, down from the one-year deferral in force since 2017.

Several of the protections and gaps above vary by canton rather than applying uniformly: conversion-therapy bans and the wording of detention placement rules are cantonal, so exposure depends partly on where in the country a person is held or treated.

The hate-crime figures cited are raw counts of reported cases with no per-capita denominator, so they indicate a direction of travel (reports up fivefold since 2020) rather than a comparative level of risk against other jurisdictions.
localsOnly:
Employers must protect employees' personal dignity under Articles 328ff. of the Code of Obligations, a duty concretised for trans people by the Equality Act (GLG). Trans staff may use their preferred name and gender at work without any official document change.

In June 2023 the Federal Supreme Court upheld a cantonal school's dismissal of a teacher who refused to call a transgender student by his chosen male first name, ruling that the school's duty to protect the student's privacy and self-determination outweighed the teacher's religious objections.

For minors, the self-declaration route originally required guardian consent for ages 12 to 18. The National Council suppressed that requirement and the Council of States set 16 as the age below which guardian consent is needed.

Conversion therapy is banned in Neuchâtel (2023), Valais and Vaud (2024), while no federal ban is in force.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific violence statistic with a denominator appears in this inventory. The hate-crime figures are LGBTIQ-wide raw reports collected through a helpline, and no comparison against the general homicide or assault rate is available here.

Whether Article 261bis covers incitement grounded on gender identity is unresolved in these sources: UNHCR states that gender-identity discrimination is prohibited, while the criminal provision and the Federal Office for Gender Equality overview are framed on sexual-orientation grounds.

The federal conversion-therapy ban adopted by the lower house on 12 December 2022 remains pending in the upper house; no adoption date or outcome is documented here.

No federal rule on the placement of trans detainees, and no case law on the subject, is documented; only the Basel-Stadt detention law text is carried, so practice in other cantons is not sourced.

The ILGA-Europe index score and per-category ratings for Switzerland are referenced but not carried in this inventory.
